extracted.intended_audience: scholars/students of humor studies, linguistics, and performance analysis (e.g., researchers analyzing stand-up comedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical framework and evaluative criteria for analyzing stand-up comedy performances (methodological choices, semantic/formal representations, pragmatic/performance features, and categories of comedic technique), illustrated via Bo Burnham's routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal semantic conversion / denotation assignment (Fda)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal semantic theory converts elements of the object-language (natural language sentences) into entities in a universal/meta-language via a denotation assignment function, Fda; e.g., 'The woman wrote a review' becomes write(cid:48)(woman(cid:48), review(cid:48)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal approach requires explicitly stating grammatical/syntactical conversion rules (e.g., GR1obj → GR1meta). The paper notes that these rules must be defined 'such that no linguistic aspect is lost' and criticizes any analysis that takes liberties by omitting explicit conversion rules. If rules like GR1obj and GR1meta are not stated, the formal conversion is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and scope of state-of-affairs (ontology composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define what the state-of-affairs (and its ontologies ORe_S and OIm_S) consists of — which persons, characters, actions, and objects are included in the representation of a joke's situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance mathematical/formal completeness (which would include every audience member, every object, etc.) against analytic relevance. The paper argues that including everything (e.g., audience member #125's glasses) would be 'more or less infinite' and confusing; instead, include elements that convey the most important aspects of the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performatives: requirements for successful execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the necessary requirements for a performative speech act (e.g., lying) to be successfully performed — for lying, being intentionally deceitful with the purpose of misleading another participant is a core requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There exists a theoretical set of exact requirements for performatives, but in practice the paper relies on 'surface level (common knowledge) requirements' to judge success. Analysts should acknowledge ambiguity and may need to state which requirements they adopt; successes may be uncertain if some audience members 'saw through' the act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (and limits) of Grice's Cooperative Principle and maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the Cooperative Principle and Gricean maxims as points of 'conversational common ground' between performer and audience to help identify where comedy is created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comedy contexts audiences expect deception and violations (Quantity, Quality, Relation, Manner), so claims that the comedian 'follows' the Cooperative Principle are misleading — the audience is under the illusion of cooperation. Analysts should therefore focus on the ways the comedian opts out of the principle (the manner of violations) rather than assuming genuine observance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership Categorization Analysis (MCA): category-bound predicates and category-activity puzzles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use MCA to analyze how categories (e.g., 'women') are associated with activities (e.g., 'bad at driving') and how combining conflicting categories and activities (category-activity puzzles) can create humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply MCA to detect contrasts produced by assigning category-bound predicates and then breaking expectations (example: portraying a protagonist as a 'tough guy' then revealing him as 'soft'). MCA helps formalize stereotype-based incongruities in jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity (subversion of expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity-based humor arises from subverting expectations — being incongruous with what the audience anticipates (e.g., an unexpected context or reversal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify setups that create expectations and then analyze how the joke subverts them (the paper cites Comey's firing at a recruitment event and Bo's deviation from storytelling norms as examples). Incongruity is central to why an audience perceives something as funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling structure as an evaluative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether a joke incorporates storytelling elements: a set of characters, a clear beginning (inciting event), a middle (tests/complications), and an end (resolution); moral is optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify material as 'story' when the narrative structure is present even if a moral is absent (Bo's story D lacks an explicit moral but still counts). Consider degree of narrative (full story vs. partial elements) when placing a comedian on a 'storyteller' spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic type / storyteller spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a comedian on a spectrum of comedic type (e.g., storyteller vs. one-liner) based on how much of their material relies on storytelling elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence and prominence of narrative material across jokes to determine placement; Bo is positioned 'in the storyteller end' because many of his jokes incorporate storytelling aspects even if he uses other techniques as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic categories / 'comedic force' taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify jokes according to categories (the paper's eleven-category scheme exemplified): character, reference, shock, parody, hyperbole, wordplay, analogy, madcap, etc.; count occurrences to determine predominant forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish primary categories (the driving force: e.g., character, reference, parody) from auxiliary categories (supporting techniques: shock, hyperbole, wordplay, analogy, madcap). Use frequency and centrality in each joke to assess a comedian's dominant comedic forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of form/convention (parodic technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody can target not only content but the conventions of a performance form (e.g., rap conventions, storytelling conventions); parody arises from mimicking and exaggerating these conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the joke parodies genre conventions (e.g., Bo parodies rap mannerisms or storytelling norms) and how that parody interacts with other categories (parody alone may not be funny but can enable humor when combined with shock or incongruity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatability / reference as central comedic resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Using common experiences or references that the audience can relate to increases comedic impact (reference category).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the joke taps into widely shared experiences (e.g., breakups, spilling liquids) and how that shared recognition sets up expectations to be subverted. Note exceptions where reference is to a general narrative form rather than a shared lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy via sabotage of audience expectation (proficiency at subversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is created by sabotaging audience expectations so they 'do not even have the slightest idea of what is going to happen' — i.e., proﬁcient subversion of conventions and familiar concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing material, identify the conventions being sabotaged and how the performer manipulates audience anticipation (timing, performative choices, role-playing, deliberate ambiguity). This criterion connects pragmatic, semantic, and performative analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-playing and character portrayal fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate when the performer is playing an extension of self versus fully embodying a fictional character — degree of identification affects interpretive analysis (e.g., rapper persona vs. fairy-tale frog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note how performances oscillate between characters that are 'an extension of oneself' and characters that are 'complete removal of oneself.' This distinction informs readings of intent, performative success, and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological trade-offs and declared liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: When using formal tools, explicitly state any liberties or methodological simplifications (e.g., not strictly converting every sentence to meta-language) and justify why focusing on characters/actions is analytically preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the loss of formal rigor when omitting grammatical conversion rules and explain the analytic rationale (paper prioritizes analysis of state-of-affairs elements relevant to the joke rather than exhaustive formal conversion). Be transparent about limits and consequences of such choices.
